```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 72)
# One BLAS thread when built on CRAN (fastkcv is single-threaded; a
# multithreaded BLAS would use several cores). Local builds keep the default.
if (!identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true") &&
  requireNamespace("RhpcBLASctl", quietly = TRUE)) {
  RhpcBLASctl::blas_set_num_threads(1)
}
```

fastkcv computes leave-one-out and k-fold cross-validation for global
kriging (every observation in the kriging neighborhood) exactly, and much
faster than refitting the kriging system once per fold. It factorizes the
covariance matrix of the observations once. Every fold's predictions and
variances then follow from small blocks of one matrix.

The interface follows `gstat::krige.cv()`: the same `formula`, `locations`,
`data`, `model`, `nfold` and `beta` arguments, and the same output
columns. Ordinary, universal and simple kriging are supported, with the
nugget, nested models and 2D geometric anisotropy of gstat variogram models.

```{r setup}
library(fastkcv)
library(gstat)
data(meuse, package = "sp")
v <- vgm(0.59, "Sph", 897, 0.05)
```

## A drop-in companion to `krige.cv()`

```{r dropin}
cv_gstat <- krige.cv(log(zinc) ~ 1, ~ x + y, meuse, model = v,
  verbose = FALSE)
cv_fast <- kcv(log(zinc) ~ 1, ~ x + y, meuse, model = v)
head(cv_fast)
all.equal(cv_gstat, cv_fast, tolerance = 1e-10)
max(abs(cv_fast$var1.pred - cv_gstat$var1.pred))
```

The output has the same kind as the input: a data.frame here, an `sf`
object for `sf` input and a `SpatialPointsDataFrame` for `sp` input.
`var1.var` is the variance of the error in predicting the held-out
observation, nugget included, as in gstat. Universal kriging re-estimates
the trend in every fold (generalized least squares), and `beta` gives
simple kriging with a known trend:

```{r ukk}
f10 <- fold_random(~ x + y, meuse, k = 10)
uk_gstat <- krige.cv(log(zinc) ~ sqrt(dist), ~ x + y, meuse, model = v,
  nfold = f10, verbose = FALSE)
uk_fast <- kcv(log(zinc) ~ sqrt(dist), ~ x + y, meuse, model = v,
  folds = f10)
max(abs(uk_fast$var1.var - uk_gstat$var1.var))
sk_fast <- kcv(log(zinc) ~ 1, ~ x + y, meuse, model = v, beta = 5.9)
```

A scalar `nfold = k` draws folds with the same call that `krige.cv()` uses,
so the same seed gives the same folds in both packages. `fold_random()`
returns that fold vector.

Local neighborhoods (`nmax`, `nmin`, `maxdist`), block kriging and
unbounded variogram models (such as `Lin` or `Pow`) are not supported and
raise an error. So do geographic coordinates and duplicate locations.

## Factorize once, cross-validate many times

The expensive part does not depend on the folds. `kcv_prepare()` does it
once; `kcv_run()` then computes the cross-validation for any fold scheme
at a fraction of the cost. `kcv(...)` is the same as
`kcv_run(kcv_prepare(...), ...)`.

```{r prepare}
p <- kcv_prepare(log(zinc) ~ sqrt(dist), ~ x + y, meuse, model = v)
p
set.seed(1)
rmse <- replicate(20, kcv_metrics(kcv_run(p, nfold = 10))$rmse)
summary(rmse)
```

The prepared object holds an n x n matrix (8 n^2 bytes) and can be saved
with `saveRDS()`.

## Fold designs

With spatially correlated data, random folds put close neighbors of every
held-out point in the training data, so the scores mostly measure
interpolation over short distances. Spatial folds hold out whole regions.
fastkcv has three fold builders, all returning a plain integer vector that
also works as `nfold` in `krige.cv()`:

* `fold_random()`: random folds, drawn as in `krige.cv()`;
* `fold_blocks()`: a regular grid of blocks over the bounding box, given
  by the number of cells (`blocks`) or their size (`size`), optionally
  grouped at random into `k` folds;
* `fold_kmeans()`: k-means clusters of the coordinates.

```{r designs}
set.seed(1)
designs <- list(
  random = fold_random(~ x + y, meuse, k = 10),
  blocks = fold_blocks(~ x + y, meuse, blocks = c(3, 4)),
  kmeans = fold_kmeans(~ x + y, meuse, k = 10)
)
sapply(designs, function(f) length(unique(f)))
do.call(rbind, lapply(designs, function(f) kcv_metrics(kcv_run(p, folds = f))))
```

`kcv_metrics()` reports the RMSE, the mean absolute error, the bias, the
mean and variance of the z-scores (ideally 0 and 1) and the coverage of the
Gaussian prediction intervals at several levels. With `by_fold = TRUE` it
gives one row per fold.

```{r plot-blocks, fig.cap = "Block folds (3 x 4 grid over the bounding box)."}
op <- par(mar = c(2, 2, 1, 1))
plot(meuse$x, meuse$y, col = designs$blocks, pch = 19, asp = 1,
  xlab = "", ylab = "")
par(op)
```

## Buffered leave-one-out

Buffered leave-one-out holds each observation out together with every
observation within a distance `buffer` of it, and predicts it from the rest.
As the radius grows past the range of spatial correlation, the scores
approach those of prediction at unsampled locations far from the data.
`buffer = 0` is ordinary leave-one-out. The column `n_heldout` gives the
size of each hold-out set.

```{r buffer}
radii <- c(0, 100, 200, 400, 800)
t(sapply(radii, function(r) {
  out <- kcv_run(p, buffer = r)
  c(radius = r, mean_heldout = mean(out$n_heldout),
    unlist(kcv_metrics(out)[c("rmse", "mean_z", "var_z", "coverage_90")]))
}))
```

Each point is a separate kriging problem with its own hold-out set, so the
cost grows with the size of the hold-out sets. `targets` restricts the
predictions to a subset of the points. The hold-out sets are still formed
from all observations, so the statistics are those of a sample of points:

```{r targets}
set.seed(2)
tg <- sample(nrow(meuse), 40)
out <- kcv_run(p, buffer = 400, targets = tg)
nrow(out)
kcv_metrics(out)[c("n", "rmse", "var_z")]
```

## Several responses

The kriging weights depend on the locations, the model, the trend and the
folds, but not on the observed values. A matrix response is therefore
cross-validated from one factorization, and each additional column costs
only a few matrix products. The output stacks one block per response and
adds a `response` column. `kcv_metrics()` then gives one row per
response:

```{r multi}
cv_metals <- kcv(cbind(log(zinc), log(copper), log(lead)) ~ 1, ~ x + y,
  meuse, model = v, folds = f10)
table(cv_metals$response)
kcv_metrics(cv_metals)[c("response", "rmse", "var_z", "coverage_90")]
```

`kcv_run(p, y = )` cross-validates new responses at the locations of a
prepared object, with its trend and model. A simulation study is one use:
here, 200 fields are simulated from the variogram model at the
observation locations, and the cross-validated z-scores and interval
coverage are compared with their nominal values. They hold on average
when the model is correct:

```{r multi-sim}
C_v <- variogramLine(v, covariance = TRUE,
  dist_vector = as.matrix(dist(meuse[, c("x", "y")])))
set.seed(3)
sims <- crossprod(chol(C_v), matrix(rnorm(nrow(meuse) * 200),
  nrow(meuse)))
m_sim <- kcv_metrics(kcv_run(p, nfold = f10, y = sims))
nrow(m_sim)
colMeans(m_sim[c("mean_z", "var_z", "coverage_80", "coverage_95")])
```

Every response must be observed at every location. A missing value in any
column is an error, because a response cannot drop its own rows.

## A precomputed covariance matrix

`kcv_engine()` takes the covariance matrix of the observations, the trend
matrix and the folds directly. Any positive definite covariance can be
used, for example one gstat cannot express. Here, with the covariance
from `gstat::variogramLine()`, it reproduces `kcv()`:

```{r engine}
D <- as.matrix(dist(meuse[, c("x", "y")]))
C <- variogramLine(v, covariance = TRUE, dist_vector = D)
y <- log(meuse$zinc)
F <- matrix(1, nrow(meuse), 1)
e <- kcv_engine(C, F, y, folds = seq_len(nrow(meuse)))
max(abs(e$pred - cv_fast$var1.pred))
```

The response can be a matrix: each column is cross-validated with the same
weights, which costs little more than a single column. As an example of a
covariance outside gstat's models, observations with known,
site-specific measurement-error variances add them to the diagonal:

```{r engine-hetero}
tau2 <- ifelse(meuse$soil == 1, 0.01, 0.1)
e2 <- kcv_engine(C + diag(tau2), F, cbind(y, log(meuse$copper)),
  folds = designs$blocks)
str(e2)
```

`kcv_engine_prepare()` and `kcv_engine_run()` split it into the two stages,
as `kcv_prepare()` and `kcv_run()` do.

## Performance, BLAS and memory

Almost all of the time goes into one dense Cholesky factorization and one
triangular inverse of the n x n covariance matrix. R hands these to its
BLAS and LAPACK libraries. The table below gives median times in seconds
on a 4-core laptop (Intel i7-6700HQ, OpenBLAS) for ordinary kriging on
simulated data (exponential model with a nugget, random folds), from the
benchmark scripts in the package sources (`inst/bench/`). Each cell gives
fastkcv's time, then `krige.cv()`'s time and the speed-up.

| n      | LOO                  | 10-fold             | 5-fold              |
|-------:|:---------------------|:--------------------|:--------------------|
| 1,000  | 0.06; 67 (1,100x)    | 0.06; 1.4 (21x)     | 0.07; 0.8 (12x)     |
| 2,000  | 0.25; 368 (1,500x)   | 0.27; 7.7 (28x)     | 0.29; 5.7 (19x)     |
| 5,000  | 2.1; ~3,500 (~1,700x)\* | 2.4; 112 (47x)  | 2.6; 85 (32x)       |
| 10,000 | 13; --               | 15; --              | 17; --              |

\* Not run: predicted from the smaller n. "--": `krige.cv()` not run
(predicted above 10 minutes).

The speed-up is largest for leave-one-out and shrinks as the folds become
fewer and larger. A refit of k folds costs about k factorizations of size
n (k - 1) / k, while fastkcv's single factorization dominates its own time
for all but a few large folds (each fold of size m adds about m^2 n
operations; at n = 3,000, the 2 folds of 2-fold cross-validation take about
as long as the factorization, 10 folds a fifth of it).

fastkcv computes exact global kriging. `krige.cv()` with a local
neighborhood (`nmax`) solves a different, approximate kriging system of
fixed size per prediction, so its time grows about linearly in n. For
10-fold cross-validation with `nmax = 50` on the same simulated data it
catches up with fastkcv at about n = 2,500 (OpenBLAS, 4 threads), at
n = 1,500 to 2,000 with the default 8 OpenBLAS threads, and below n = 1,000
with the reference BLAS. Its time also grows with the number of folds:
local leave-one-out took 39 s at n = 4,000, against 0.8 s for fastkcv
(OpenBLAS) and 23 s with the reference BLAS.
DiceKriging, which uses the same closed-form leave-one-out formulas, is
compared in the section "Related packages". With the reference BLAS every
method is slower, and fastkcv's
gain over `krige.cv()` is still about 600x for leave-one-out at
n = 1,000 and 2.5x to 6x for 5 to 10 folds at n = 1,000 to 5,000. At
n = 20,000, `kcv()` takes about 110 seconds.

Several responses share the factorization. At n = 5,000 (OpenBLAS), 100
responses take 2.7 s (leave-one-out) to 3.6 s (buffered, radius 50) in one
`kcv()` call, 2 to 5 ms per additional response. One `kcv()` call per
response takes 233 to 317 s.

The reference BLAS that ships with many R builds is single-threaded and
much slower on these operations than an optimized BLAS such as OpenBLAS,
Intel MKL or Apple's Accelerate. Check which one R uses with
`extSoftVersion()["BLAS"]`; see `?kcv` (section "Performance") for how to
switch. The many small matrix operations of buffered leave-one-out do not
benefit from BLAS threads. OpenBLAS starts one thread per logical CPU; on
CPUs with simultaneous multithreading, one thread per physical core can be
much faster (`OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=4` on the 4-core, 8-thread laptop above:
1.6 to 2 times faster for 10-fold `kcv()` at n = 1,500 to 5,000). The
table above used the default 8 threads.

`kcv()` builds the covariance matrix in place and needs one n x n matrix
(8 n^2 bytes: 0.8 GB at n = 10,000, 3.2 GB at n = 20,000); its measured
peak memory use above R's own baseline is within 2% of that at
n = 20,000. `kcv_engine()`
copies the user's matrix and needs two. The requirement is checked before
anything is allocated, against `getOption("fastkcv.max_gb", 6.4)` GB; raise
the option on machines with more memory.

## Related packages

fastkcv is a companion to gstat, not a fork or a replacement. `kcv()` takes
the inputs of `krige.cv()` and returns its output, and fitting the
variogram and kriging new locations stay with gstat. It is a separate
package for three reasons:

* The single factorization works only for global kriging, where every
  fold shares one covariance matrix of the observations. gstat's engine
  sets up a kriging system for each prediction location, which is what
  makes local neighborhoods (`nmax`, `nmin`, `maxdist`) possible; with
  local neighborhoods every point has its own system and there is nothing
  to factorize once.
* It needs compiled C++ code (Rcpp, RcppArmadillo) and a dense n x n
  matrix (8 n^2 bytes), which is checked before anything is allocated.
* Most of the package is a cross-validation toolkit rather than a faster
  `krige.cv()`: buffered leave-one-out, spatial fold builders,
  `kcv_metrics()`, `kcv_prepare()` / `kcv_run()` to reuse one
  factorization across fold designs, and `kcv_engine()` for any covariance
  matrix.

`leaveOneOut.km()` in DiceKriging uses the same closed-form leave-one-out
algebra. It has no nugget term, works with tensor-product kernels on a
design matrix rather than gstat variogram models on spatial data, and
offers neither k-fold nor buffered designs. Without a nugget, and from the
same covariance matrix, the two give the same variances (to about 1e-15)
and predictions that agree to about 1e-13, for simple kriging and for
ordinary kriging with the trend re-estimated in each fold. The exception is
the smoother `matern5_2` kernel with ordinary kriging: without a nugget its
covariance matrix is badly conditioned, and the predictions agree only to
between 1e-9 and 1e-7. End to
end (model setup plus leave-one-out), fastkcv is 1.6 to 4.1 times faster
with OpenBLAS and 1.4 to 2.1 times with the reference BLAS. On the
leave-one-out step alone the two are about level (0.9 to 1.8 times with
OpenBLAS, 0.75 to 0.9 times with the reference BLAS).

blockCV and spatialsample build spatial folds (blocks, clusters, buffers,
nearest-neighbor distance matching) for any model, but do not fit or
predict with one. A partition from them, such as `folds_ids` from
blockCV's `cv_spatial()`, can be passed to `kcv_run(folds = )`.

|                                | LOO              | k-fold | Buffered LOO | Block / cluster folds | Nugget, gstat models | Input                  | Exact, no refit per fold |
|:-------------------------------|:-----------------|:-------|:-------------|:----------------------|:---------------------|:-----------------------|:-------------------------|
| fastkcv                        | yes              | yes    | yes          | yes                   | yes                  | data.frame, `sf`, `sp` | yes                      |
| gstat `krige.cv()`             | yes              | yes    | no           | any fold vector       | yes                  | data.frame, `sf`, `sp` | no (refits)              |
| DiceKriging `leaveOneOut.km()` | yes              | no     | no           | no                    | no                   | design matrix          | yes                      |
| blockCV                        | NNDM variant     | yes    | yes          | yes                   | (folds only)         | `sf`, `sp` points      | (folds only)             |
| spatialsample                  | yes (`v = Inf`)  | yes    | yes          | yes                   | (folds only)         | `sf`                   | (folds only)             |

"(folds only)": the package returns fold assignments and fits no model.
NNDM is nearest-neighbor distance matching (`cv_nndm()`), a variant of
leave-one-out; blockCV's buffered leave-one-out is `cv_buffer()`.
spatialsample's buffered leave-one-out is `spatial_buffer_vfold_cv()` with
`v = Inf` and a `buffer`.
